Replacing turf that predates the state's current rule

Turf replacement in Harmony prices close to a new installation at the $8–$18 range, minus whatever base can be reused, as of September 2026. Because Harmony's original neighborhoods opened around 2003, a replacement job here often means correcting a base or infill built before the state's May 2026 material standard existed.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have 825 sq ft of turf original to the early 2000s

Replacing 825 sq ft of turf original to one of Harmony's earliest lawns, assuming the base needs a full rebuild rather than a reuse, prices between $6,600 and $14,850 at the $8–$18 range, with most jobs this size landing near $8,250 to $13,200 using the typical $10–$16 band. That estimate assumes the crew finds unwashed fill or a settled base once the old turf comes up, which is common enough on an installation this old that it's worth budgeting for rather than assuming the existing rock will pass inspection.

An older lawn built to a different set of assumptions

Turf installed when Harmony's founding neighborhoods were new, if any dates that far back, went in years before Florida's synthetic turf standard set requirements for washed base material and restricted infill to natural products. A replacement project on a lawn that old is a natural point to check whether the original infill was ever crumb rubber or another synthetic material now barred outside a playground's footprint, since a full tear-out is the easiest time to correct that rather than layering new turf over an outdated base.

Specifying more UV stability for a corner lot's sun-heavy side

A Harmony corner lot often has one frontage that catches more direct afternoon sun than the interior side of the property, and a replacement is a reasonable point to specify a more UV-stable product for that exposed frontage specifically, rather than ordering one uniform spec for the whole lot. The two sides were never going to age at the same rate anyway, so matching product choice to actual sun exposure, rather than treating the property as a single environment, is a more direct way to even out how the two sides wear over the coming years.

Deciding what base survives the tear-out

Not every old base needs full replacement. If the original crushed rock was washed material that's held its shape and still drains, a replacement job can sometimes reuse that layer with a fresh compaction pass rather than hauling it out entirely. A base that's crusted over from unwashed fill or settled unevenly after two decades doesn't get that option, and the difference between the two usually only becomes clear once the old turf is pulled back.

A base that looks flat but was never washed to begin with

An older Harmony lawn's base can appear level and well-compacted on the surface while still holding a fines crust from subgrade material that was never washed before the original install, years before the current standard required it. That crust doesn't announce itself as a problem until the turf above it is pulled up during a replacement, at which point it's clear the base was never actually draining the way it looked like it was. Flat isn't the same as functional, which is why we check for a crust, not just for slope, before deciding a base can stay.

Old infill left mixed into a new install

Skipping a full infill removal during a Harmony replacement, especially where old crumb rubber or another synthetic infill was spread across a general lawn area, risks leaving that material mixed into the new build rather than confined to where it's actually allowed. A new installation that still has old rubber infill scattered through it hasn't actually corrected the mismatch it was supposed to fix, and it can be hard to tell from the surface that any of the old material is still present once new turf covers it.

Re-surveying the water setback as part of the pre-demo walk

A Harmony property's exact distance from a pond or canal is worth re-confirming against the current property line as part of a replacement's pre-demo walk, rather than trusting where the old turf's edge happened to sit, since the old footprint may never have been measured accurately in the first place or may have shifted slightly over years of edge repairs. Settling that measurement before demo starts, rather than assuming the existing edge was correct, is what lets the new footprint land on the real setback line instead of just repeating an old guess.

Watching a corrected footprint for a new drainage low point

Moving a Harmony lawn's edge outside a live oak's drip line or farther back from a setback line during replacement changes where water moves across that section of yard, even when the correction itself was overdue and necessary. The boundary where the new, adjusted footprint meets the older, unchanged part of the lawn is worth watching through the first few storms, since a grade change at that line can create a small low point that wasn't there under the old layout until the new one settles in fully.

Why replacement pricing tracks close to new installation

A replacement job carries most of the same steps a first installation does, demolition, base work, seaming and edging, minus only the sod-removal step a first-time conversion needs. That's why turf replacement tends to price near the same $8–$18 range as a new lawn rather than at a discount, with the final number depending mostly on how much of the old base survives inspection.

Questions people ask

Does replacing turf in Harmony trigger a new Residential Owners Association review?

A straightforward like-for-like replacement usually doesn't need a fresh submission, but a change in color, pile height or the edged footprint should go through the association's design review the same as a first-time installation would.

How do I know if my old Harmony lawn's infill is compliant with the 2026 rule?

The clearest way is a visual and material check once the turf is pulled back during a replacement quote; rubber infill has a distinct look and feel compared with sand or zeolite, and an installer can usually tell within minutes of exposing it.
